newsitem.title: USA: PLATINUM MARKET SEEN IN DEFICIT IN 1997 - CPM.
newsitem.headline: PLATINUM MARKET SEEN IN DEFICIT IN 1997 - CPM.

text.p: The platinum market is likely to swing into a supply/demand deficit in 1997 for the first time since 1985, while the palladium market surplus is seen shrinking as supplies contract for the first time since 1988, New York-based industry consultants CPM Group said in its 1997 platinum group metal (PGM) market survey published Monday.
Platinum prices have already seen seven-year highs this year, with palladium at a 17-year peak, due to the suspension of Russian platinum group metal (PGM) exports for five months.

"Once Russian exports come back into the market, prices could experience a sharp sell off, although the breadth of the correction is expected to be limited by continued tightness of physical supplies," CPM managing director Jeffrery Christian said at a briefing for analysts.
"Russian exports now are expected to resume by early July," Christian said.
Earlier this month, Russian officials said PGM exports would likely resume in late June.
CPM Group estimates Russian platinum exports at 750,000 ounces in 1997, a decline of at least 25 percent from around one million ounces in 1996.
But "this figure could prove to be too high, depending on the level of these shipments," Christian said.
Russian palladium exports are forecast to be around three million ounces this year, down 24 percent from 3.95 million in 1996.

Fabrication demand is outpacing new platinum supply in 1997 and the shortfall in supplies is projected at 326,000 ounces, the first deficit in 12 years, but it could prove even greater depending on the volume of Russian supplies, the CPM report said.

Total platinum fabrication demand is projected at 5.38 million ounces, an increase of 6.9 percent, while new supplies, including Russian exports, are expected to slide 1.1 percent to 5.05 million ounces.
While Russian exports of platinum are seen declining, other mine production is forecast to rise 4.7 percent to 3.88 million ounces.

Output in South Africa, the world's largest producer of platinum, is seen rising 3.4 percent to 3.53 million ounces, while Canadian production is projected at 150,000 ounces, up 5,000 ounces from 1996.
Production in remaining countries is seen up 37 percent to 200,000 ounces, largely reflecting the startup of the Hartley Mine in Zimbabwe and the expansion of the Stillwater Mine in the U.S.
On the demand side, platinum use in jewelry is projected at 2.08 million ounces in 1997, up 15.8 percent from last year.

Autocatalyst demand is seen rising one percent to 1.73 million ounces, while electronics demand for platinum could rise 5.5 percent to 250,000 ounces, and platinum use in chemical and petroleum catalysts is forecast at 219,000 ounces, up 2.8 percent.
Demand for platinum from the medical and dental sectors is seen rising 2.1 percent to 49,000 ounces.
Finally, the U.S. Mint's launch of the U.S. platinum Eagle coin this year is expected to increase investment demand for platinum by about 200,000 ounces.
Meanwhile, the surplus of new mine supply of palladium relative to fabrication demand is expected to narrow to 628,000 ounces from 1.64 million ounces last year.
Total supply is projected at 6.58 million ounces, down 10.2 pct, largely due to lower Russian supplies, while consumption is seen increasing 4.6 pct to 5.96 million ounces.
Russian production is seen around 2.50 million ounces in 1997, though supplies from stockpiles may result in total exports of around three million ounces.

Mine production of palladium outside of Russia is seen climbing eight percent to 2.37 million ounces in 1997, largely due to increases in output from South African mining houses, Amplats and Impala, CPM said.
Palladium use in electronics, accounting for about half of palladium demand, according to CPM Group, is expected to rise 10.5 pct to 2.94 million ounces.

Meanwhile, palladium use in autocatalysts is seen up only 0.3 pct at 953,000 ounces, though CPM Group admits autocatalyst demand for palladium rose 51.5 pct last year as the auto industry worldwide began using higher loadings of the metal in autocatalysts.
But the key to the palladium market in 1997 will be the timing of the Russian return to the market and the amount Russia will export, CPM Group said.

"As the world's largest producer of palladium, accounting for about 54 percent of refined metal entering the international market in 1996, Russia's interruption in palladium exports forced numerous dealers and end-users to search aggressively for stocks.
After exporting more than it produced from its mines, Russian stockpiles of palladium could now be down to 1.5 to 2.0 million ounces, Christian said.
Meanwhile, its platinum stockpiles are estimated to have fallen to around 0.5-1.0 million ounces, he said.
((Clive McKeef, New York Commodities Desk, 212-859-1641))
